idiom_name: sync.Mutex-guarded primary fields, dirty bool and cached value
implementation_notes: Go has no properties, so the pattern is method discipline: a struct keeps the primary fields, the cached derived value and a dirty bool, every mutator sets the flag, and the accessor recomputes and clears it while holding a sync.Mutex. The Go memory model makes unsynchronised access to that bool a data race that `go build -race` reports (and race-free programs are sequentially consistent), so a shared flag needs a mutex or the sync/atomic package; a mutex is the safe default and the standard-library documentation itself prefers channels or sync over bare atomics. sync.Once/sync.OnceValue replace the flag for the one-shot case but can never be reset, so they serve lazy initialisation, not invalidation.
pitfalls: A plain bool read and written by several goroutines is a data race; without the mutex the compiler and CPU may keep stale values in registers, and the race detector reports it.
Copying a struct that contains a sync.Mutex (or an atomic value after first use) splits the lock; pass pointers and run `go vet`, which flags it.
The mutex is not reentrant: holding it while the recomputation calls back into the same object, or into another locked object, deadlocks.
sync.Once cannot be reset, so a mutex-guarded recomputation must not be replaced by OnceValue when invalidation is needed.

variants.name: Atomic publication with a lock-free fast path
variants.idiom_name: atomic.Bool dirty flag plus atomic.Pointer[T] cached value
variants.implementation_notes: Go 1.19 added the typed atomics (atomic.Bool, atomic.Pointer[T], ...) that hide the unsafe.Pointer conversions and force every access through the atomic API; they make a lock-free read path practical. The flag and the published value are a pair: writers rebuild under a mutex, store the new value, then clear the flag; readers check the flag first and only take the lock when it is set, which is correct because Go's atomics are sequentially consistent (the Go memory model aligns with C/C++/Java/Rust/Swift) and the store-then-clear order establishes the publication. The cached value must be immutable after publication, since readers use it without holding the lock.
pitfalls: The typed atomics must not be copied after first use (`go vet` reports it), and an atomic.Pointer value must be zero-initialised rather than assigned a struct copy.
Order is the contract: storing the flag false before the pointer publishes a clean flag over the old value; readers may then never rebuild.
The published value must be treated as immutable - mutating it in place after Store is a data race, so rebuild a fresh value and store it.
A nil pointer is the initial dirty state; a reader that forgets the flag check dereferences nil, so the constructor must publish an initial value or the fast path must test for nil.
